title: Electrode potentials and the SHE; Commercial cells and fuel cells
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX06#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX06#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX06#t4 term and clue written for the game; RX04#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: RX04#N.4a, RX06#N.3a, RX04#N.10a, RX06#N.6a, RX04#N.13, RX06#N.8, RX06#N.10, RX06#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Anion
items.clue: Negative particle such as NO₃⁻, moving into the zinc side as Zn²⁺ builds up.

items.label: Cation
items.clue: Positive particle such as K⁺, moving into the copper side as Cu²⁺ is used up.

items.label: Fuel cell
items.clue: Device fed continuously with H₂ and O₂; it never needs electrical recharging.

items.label: Potential difference
items.clue: What is measured between two half-cells; one half-cell alone can never give a reading.

questions.stem: Why is the standard electrode potential of the hydrogen half-cell, 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g), given as 0 V?

options.text: No oxidation or reduction occurs at the hydrogen electrode.
Its absolute potential has been measured directly and found to be zero.
It is assigned by convention as the reference for other half-cells.
The platinum electrode is inert, so no potential develops.

questions.explanation: Only potential differences can be measured, so one half-cell must be chosen as the reference and given a value. By convention it is the SHE, at 0 V.

questions.stem: A cell is made from Zn(s)|Zn²⁺(aq) and Cu(s)|Cu²⁺(aq) half-cells joined by a salt bridge containing KNO₃(aq). Zinc is oxidised. Which describes how charge moves through the salt bridge?

options.text: Electrons move through it from the zinc half-cell to the copper half-cell.
NO₃⁻ ions move to the copper half-cell, attracted by its positive electrode.
Zn²⁺ ions pass through it to be deposited on the copper electrode.
K⁺ ions move to the copper half-cell and NO₃⁻ ions to the zinc half-cell.

questions.explanation: Zn²⁺ is produced on the zinc side and Cu²⁺ removed on the copper side. NO₃⁻ and K⁺ move to keep both neutral.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potentials: Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s), E° = −2.37 V · Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s), E° = −0.76 V · Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s), E° = +0.34 V · Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ ⇌ Ag(s), E° = +0.80 V. Which species is the strongest oxidising agent?

options.text: Mg²⁺(aq), as its E° value is the largest in size
Mg(s), as it is the species most readily oxidised
Ag⁺(aq), as its E° value is the most positive
Ag(s), as silver has the most positive E° value

questions.explanation: Ag⁺ (+0.80 V) accepts electrons most readily, so it is the strongest oxidising agent listed.

questions.stem: A nickel–cadmium cell is rechargeable. While it is being charged, the reaction at its positive electrode is: Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻ → NiO(OH) + H₂O + e⁻. Which half-equation shows the reaction at this electrode while the cell is in use (discharge)?

options.text: Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻ + e⁻ → NiO(OH) + H₂O
NiO(OH) + H₂O → Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻ + e⁻
Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻ → NiO(OH) + H₂O + e⁻
NiO(OH) + H₂O + e⁻ → Ni(OH)₂ + OH⁻

questions.explanation: Discharge is charging run backwards: every product becomes a reactant, electrons included. Ni +3 → +2 is reduction, as expected at the positive electrode.

questions.stem: A standard Pb²⁺/Pb half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter reads 0.13 V. The lead electrode is the negative electrode. Which statement is correct?

options.text: E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = +0.13 V, because the voltmeter reading gives the lead electrode's potential directly, sign included.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V, which is the absolute potential of the lead electrode on its own.
E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V; the reading is the difference from the hydrogen electrode, which is 0 V by convention.
No reaction happens at the hydrogen electrode, because its E° is 0 V.

questions.explanation: A single half-cell cannot be measured alone. The SHE is defined as 0 V, so the whole 0.13 V is assigned to lead; lead is oxidised (it supplies the electrons), so its E° is negative.

questions.stem: Which half-equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode of an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?

options.text: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻
2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻

questions.explanation: Hydrogen is oxidised (0 → +1), releasing electrons into the circuit at the negative electrode. Atoms and charge balance (−2 each side).

questions.stem: Which statement about fuel cells, non-rechargeable cells and rechargeable cells is correct?

options.text: A fuel cell supplies electricity for as long as its fuel and oxygen are supplied.
A rechargeable cell stores electricity, which it releases unchanged when used.
A hydrogen fuel cell produces only water, so using one causes no pollution of any kind.
A fuel cell burns its fuel and converts the heat released to electrical energy.

questions.explanation: Its reactants are fed in continuously and products removed, so it doesn't run down like a cell with a fixed amount of reactants.

questions.stem: A car's lead–acid battery is recharged by the engine many times. During use, solid lead(II) sulfate forms on both electrodes: Pb(s) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2e⁻ PbO₂(s) + 4H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l) Why can this battery be recharged?

options.text: Its sulfuric acid stores electricity, which the engine tops up.
The PbSO₄ stays on the electrodes, so a current can turn it back into Pb and PbO₂.
Charging runs the same two reactions again, only faster.
Lead atoms never lose electrons, so the cell is never used up.

questions.explanation: The products stay where they formed. An external current drives both half-equations backwards, re-forming the reactants.
